title: DFS in Helsinki: find the path—go deep!
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) “go deep” through Helsinki’s Kallio street graph to discover a route. This visualization shows how exploring neighbors recursively can lead to fast discoveries—or detours—depending on traversal order.
ig_caption:
🧭💡 DFS on real street maps: Helsinki (Kallio) edition!

Depth-First Search (DFS) explores a graph by taking one neighbor path as far as possible before backtracking. In graph-theory terms, you’re traversing an adjacency list of intersections (nodes) connected by streets (edges), using a stack-like recursion strategy to visit reachable vertices in a depth-first order. ⚙️

✨ Key takeaway from the visualization: DFS doesn’t guarantee the shortest route—it prioritizes depth based on neighbor ordering, which can dramatically change the path you see.

📍We mapped the idea onto a realistic grid/graph layout resembling city streets, so each “decision” is a choice of which adjacent node to expand next.

👉 Want a follow-up video for BFS, Dijkstra, or A* on the same map? Drop “NEXT” in the comments and share this reel with a fellow coder! 🚀
fb_caption:
🗺️ Depth-First Search (DFS) in Helsinki (Kallio)! 🌿

DFS is a graph search method that goes deep into one path, then backtracks when it can’t proceed—so it’s all about exploring connectivity in a depth-first order. In this visualization, intersections are nodes and streets are edges, and you can see how traversal choices affect the route found. If you enjoyed it, share this post with your study group and comment what algorithm you want next!
